item.title: Three People Are Killed at a Minnesota Day Care Center
item.description:
Two adults and a child were killed Wednesday morning at a small day care center in a Minneapolis suburb, police officials said.

The three victims were members of a family, Brent Johnson, the police chief in Hopkins, Minn., told reporters. The assailant, a man, was among those who died, Chief Johnson said.

Chief Johnson called the attack a domestic situation and said investigators did not believe there was a continuing threat. The killings happened around 9 a.m., he said. Chief Johnson said that investigators believe that the two adults who died owned the day care, which operated inside their home.

Six other children who were at the in-home day care center were reunited with their parents, he said.

“This is a horrific, tragic situation for any community, especially here in Hopkins, where we don’t see this type of crime,” Chief Johnson said.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: 3 Ex-Georgia Deputies Used Flock Cameras to Stalk People, Sheriff Says
item.description:
Three former Georgia sheriff’s deputies have been arrested on charges that they used Flock cameras to stalk people, the latest cases to raise concerns about potential abuse involving the widely used network of license-plate readers.

The Bibb County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement that an internal audit conducted with help from Flock revealed that the deputies had used the camera system’s license plate data for “personal, non-law-enforcement purposes.”

All three were involved in separate incidents tracking people with whom they had a “personal relationship at the time,” the sheriff’s office said.

The deputies were arrested on Monday on charges that included stalking, prohibited use of license plate data and violating their oaths as public officers. They have since been released on bond.

Two of those charged, Toni Lewis and Coznavian Stubbs, resigned from their positions as patrol deputies during the investigation, and the third, Joseph Callaway, resigned as a K-9 deputy shortly after his arrest, the office said.

The Bibb County sheriff, David Davis, said that a tool that Flock introduced in April, called Audit Assistance, had uncovered the deputies’ misuse of the system. Flock says the tool continuously monitors system activity and flags search patterns that “fall outside an agency’s typical usage,” allowing police departments to identify instances of potential abuse.

“I was saddened by it,” Sheriff Davis said in an interview on Wednesday. “Each one of these deputies were good deputies who had been here for several years and were doing a good job. However, they made some poor decisions and crossed the line.”

Mr. Stubbs said on Wednesday that he had been accused of using Flock cameras to stalk his girlfriend but that he had only used the system to look up the license plate on his own car. The case, he said, had been “blown way out” of proportion.

Mr. Callaway declined to comment on the charges. Ms. Lewis could not be reached at phone numbers listed under her name, and it was not immediately clear if she had a lawyer.

A national debate has been brewing over Flock cameras, which can be found on roads in every state but Alaska. About 7,000 law enforcement agencies, or 40 percent of all departments in the United States, have contracts with the company, which is based in Atlanta.

Flock’s cameras, which use artificial intelligence to automatically identify and track vehicles, are connected, creating a vast, searchable network. Investigators have praised the system as a valuable tool that helps them track down stolen cars, find missing or wanted people and solve crimes

Critics, including local watchdog groups and civil liberties organizations, have said the cameras create an umbrella of surveillance that can be easily misused.

In Milwaukee, an officer was charged with using camera data to track someone he was dating and the person’s ex. In Texas, an officer used the cameras to track a woman across state lines who was suspected of self-administering an abortion. In Georgia, a former Polk County officer was charged last week with using the camera system “for non-law-enforcement purposes.” Other officers across the country have been disciplined or fired for tracking romantic partners.

In Bibb County, Ga., which is home to about 158,000 people and includes Macon, Sheriff Davis announced in June 2023 that his office had been awarded a $1.6 million state grant to deploy Flock cameras and to set up a Strategic Information Center to monitor the license-plate data they collect.

Sheriff Davis said that at one more than 220 deputies had access to the cameras, but that number had since been cut to around 160. He said he planned to work with community members to ensure the system is only used for legitimate investigations.

“We will continue to monitor and audit the use of this technology and take appropriate action whenever those standards are violated,” Sheriff Davis said in a statement. “Protecting the public also means protecting the public’s trust.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Two Killed in Military Helicopter Crash Near Fort Hood in Texas
item.description:
Two people died in a military helicopter crash on Wednesday outside Fort Hood in Texas, the authorities said.

The Bell County Sheriff’s Office received a 911 call just after 1:30 p.m. about a helicopter crash in Salado, a small town about 20 miles southeast of Fort Hood, a United States Army base.

The two people were pronounced dead around 2:30 p.m. local time, said Cliff Coleman, a spokesman for the sheriff’s office. He directed questions about the identity of the two people to the military.

“You could tell it was a violent crash,” Mr. Coleman said.

Officials at Fort Hood did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a news release, U.S. Army officials said the aircraft involved in the crash, an AH-64 Apache attack helicopter, was based at Fort Hood.

The crash caused a blaze in the dry fields where it landed and law enforcement officials evacuated several area residents, Mr. Coleman said.

The fire was not immediately contained, he said.

A number of military helicopters have crashed in Texas in recent decades. In 2015, four soldiers died when a Black Hawk helicopter crashed about 60 miles north of Austin. In 2004, a brigadier general and six soldiers in Texarkana, Texas, also aboard a Black Hawk, crashed into a transmission tower and died.

item.title: Woman Arrested After Confessing to Starting Nevada Fire, Officials Say
item.description:
A woman was arrested after she told firefighters that she had intentionally set fires that became part of a larger blaze that is still burning along the border of California and Nevada, the authorities said Tuesday.

The woman, Christine Mitchell, 47, was arrested on suspicion of third-degree arson and possession of less than 14 grams of a controlled substance, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office in Nevada said in a statement on Tuesday. Ms. Mitchell’s public defender didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Mitchell left a home near Freds Mountain Road and set multiple fires, the sheriff’s office said. She caught the attention of firefighters who were responding to the resulting blaze, known as the Fred Mountain fire, and told them she had meant to start the fire.

The Fred Mountain fire, which is burning north of Reno, Nev., has since merged with another nearby wildfire, known as the Bug fire. The Bug fire has covered more than 70,000 acres and has forced thousands of people to evacuate, including from tribal land. It’s one of many large wildfires burning in the western United States during a fire season that has been unusually active for much of the region.

Ms. Mitchell was taken into custody on Sunday. Senior Judge Derek Dreiling at the Reno Justice Court set her bail at $80,000 on Tuesday, according to court records.

The sheriff’s office did not explain what the authorities believed Ms. Mitchell’s motive might have been for starting the fires.

The Reno-Sparks Indian Colony declared an emergency in response to the fires, and its Hungry Valley community was evacuated. Another large blaze east of the Bug fire, called the Stallion fire, is threatening Pyramid Lake Paiute tribal land. The Stallion fire, which officials said was caused by a human, was not contained as of Wednesday morning.

“We understand our Hungry Valley residents are frustrated,” Bethany Sam, a spokeswoman for Reno-Sparks Indian Colony, said during a Facebook livestream Tuesday night. “We know you all want to come home, check on your property, take care of your animals and get back to your normal lives.”

Gov. Joe Lombardo of Nevada also declared a state of emergency on Monday, citing a shortage of wildland fire resources as several wildfires burned across the region.

This week, the Federal Emergency Management Agency authorized the use of federal funds to help Nevada fight the fires.

item.title: Hegseth Says Anti-Cartel Coalition Will Do ‘Bad Things to Bad People’
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called on military leaders in Latin America on Wednesday to ramp up their fight against drug traffickers and join the U.S. military in operations against cartels.

Mr. Hegseth, speaking to civilian defense leaders and top generals from 18 other countries at a meeting of a U.S.-led counter-cartel coalition in Panama, doubled down on the Trump administration’s pledge to use military force in addition to law enforcement measures to combat drug traffickers.

The collective goal is “to degrade, dismantle and destroy narco-terrorist networks,” said Mr. Hegseth, speaking on the sidelines of a major U.S.-led regional training exercise in Panama.

With his typical bravado, Mr. Hegseth said the cartel-busting coalition’s motto would be, “We do bad things to bad people.”

The Trump administration has in recent months stepped up its cooperation with allies across Latin America to combat the drug trade. It created the coalition, part of the regional Shield of the Americas alliance, and convened its first meeting in March.

That month, Ecuador and the United States launched joint military operations against designated terrorist groups. In May, the Pentagon pressed Guatemala to agree to joint U.S. airstrikes and other military action inside its borders to target suspected drug groups.

Mr. Hegseth said on Wednesday that Honduras and Colombia had also agreed to allow joint operations.

Last week, the military’s U.S. Southern Command announced Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, setting up the infrastructure for an expansion of its war against drugs in cooperation with regional allies.

This new task force builds on a yearlong Pentagon campaign in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, where the military has conducted 66 boat strikes that have killed at least 221 people who it says, without presenting evidence, were trafficking drugs.

Legal experts have warned that the strikes are illegal, because the military cannot deliberately target civilians who are not directly participating in hostilities, even if they are breaking the law. Trafficking drugs, they say, does not rise to the standard of hostilities.

On Wednesday, Mr. Hegseth asserted that these strikes have decreased the number of suspected drug vessels by more than half in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific. But a recent investigation by The New York Times revealed that cocaine, by far the top drug smuggled out of South America, is as easy to get in much of the United States as it was before the strikes began.

The United States also recently announced it was fast-tracking military cooperation with Colombia, where voters elected a right-wing president in June. The country could emerge as a key piece of the U.S. push against traffickers and organized crime in the region.

Colombia is the world’s largest producer of cocaine and has in the past been a staunch U.S. ally.

For the last four years, however, relations between the two countries grew strained as Colombia’s leftist former president, Gustavo Petro, spoke out frequently against President Trump’s boat strikes and other policies toward the region.

For decades, U.S. policy in Latin America has centered on counternarcotics. Billions have been spent on military assistance, crop eradication and more; leaders have pressed for hard-line security measures and extradition agreements.

In his second term, Mr. Trump has gone further, treating drug traffickers not as criminals but as enemy combatants.

Blaming cartels and drug gangs for America’s overdose crisis and for fueling violent crime, the Trump administration has added around 20 groups to its list of foreign terrorist organizations since 2025 — from major Mexican cartels to Ecuadorean drug gangs — and has authorized using lethal force against them.

Last year, Mr. Trump justified the military’s strikes on small boats by claiming that the United States was engaged in a formal “armed conflict” with traffickers that had been designated as terrorist organizations, and that smugglers for such groups were “unlawful combatants.”

The military’s most recent strike, which killed eight people, was on June 21. Pentagon officials say there has been a pause since then partly because military teams and equipment were diverted to help provide humanitarian relief to victims of the recent earthquake in Venezuela.

Now the Trump administration appears to be moving its efforts targeting armed groups in Latin America from international waters onto land.

To date, 18 countries have joined the Pentagon-led counter-cartel coalition: Argentina, the Bahamas, Belize, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Jamaica, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Trinidad and Tobago.

The head of Southern Command, Gen. Francis Donovan, said in an online post on Aug. 3 that the coalition’s new task force would “take the fight to the enemy.”

Mr. Hegseth met with officials in Panama City during a visit in April 2025 and signed a bilateral security agreement with Panama’s president, José Raúl Mulino, a conservative who has been eager to negotiate with the Trump administration after facing threats over the Panama Canal. Panama does not have an active military.

Nations that do not officially have agreements with the United States have nevertheless been the sites of highly publicized operations since Mr. Trump took office last year.

Mr. Trump applauded a C.I.A.-involved strike early this year in Mexico that helped kill Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, the leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, one of the world’s most powerful drug trafficking organizations.

Mr. Trump also celebrated a strike in Venezuela that killed a leader of Tren de Aragua, a transnational group that he says has invaded the United States and perpetrated murders and other violence.

Experts say that organized crime and trafficking have expanded across the region in places where the government is absent and that illicit activities have spiked since the pandemic.

They caution, however, that past U.S.-led “drug wars” in the region have failed to curb the drug trade — and note that today, much of South America’s cocaine heads to Europe, not the United States.

Human rights groups also warn that militarizing the fight against armed groups risks increasing violence that threatens civilians.

Notably absent from the regional anti-trafficking alliance — and the conference in Panama this week — is Mexico, home to formidable cartels that traffic fentanyl and other deadly drugs into the United States. Like Brazil, which is not in the regional alliance either, Mexico is led by a left-wing leader, Claudia Sheinbaum.

Wary of the public backlash in a country with a long history of U.S. military intervention, and determined to protect Mexican sovereignty, Ms. Sheinbaum has stuck to a simple message: “Coordination but not subordination.”

]]>

item.title: ICE Agent Who Pushed Activist to the Ground Pleads Guilty
item.description:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor battery charge on Wednesday for throwing an activist to the ground near Chicago last year during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the region.

A judge in Cook County, Ill., sentenced the agent, Adam Saracco, to 12 months of supervision on Wednesday and ordered him not to have contact with the activist he had clashed with, Robert Held.

Mr. Saracco, 41, was charged with misdemeanor battery earlier this year after the altercation in December. At a gas station in Brookfield, Ill., Mr. Held was filming Mr. Saracco when Mr. Saracco approached him. Mr. Saracco took Mr. Held’s phone and threw him to the ground. Mr. Saracco was off duty at the time and was getting gas after leaving a nearby immigration detention center. Mr. Held said he did not sustain any injuries.

It was not clear whether Mr. Saracco was still employed by ICE. Neither Mr. Saracco nor the Department of Homeland Security responded to requests for comment on Wednesday.

Mr. Held, a trust and estate lawyer, joined many Illinois residents in protesting against ICE last fall amid a surge in immigration arrests across the Chicago area, which the Trump administration called Operation Midway Blitz.

“I am pleased that there is some accountability,” Mr. Held, 68, said in an interview on Wednesday. He added that he remained “deeply troubled and concerned” by the actions of federal agents.

“This resolution represents an important step for accountability and shows that Cook County will not turn a blind eye to unlawful conduct, no matter who you are,” Eileen O’Neill Burke, the state’s attorney for Cook County, said in a statement on Wednesday.

Ms. Burke said that her office would seek justice on behalf of those harmed during the Trump administration’s crackdown in the Chicago area “when the evidence and the law allow us to prosecute.” There have been very few local prosecutions of immigration agents.

item.title: A Fight Over Abortion and Surrogacy Ends With a Baby Born in Texas
item.description:
A bitter confrontation over surrogacy, abortion and parental rights that stretched across three states culminated on Wednesday with the birth of the baby at the center of the conflict at a Dallas hospital.

The fate of the baby, who has a severe birth defect, became a cause this summer among anti-abortion activists, who provided legal representation for the surrogate, McKenna West, and helped her travel to Texas for medical care. This week, she also received support from the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, who took legal action to compel medical treatments for the newborn.

The dispute began in the spring after the discovery at around 20 weeks of pregnancy that the fetus had a rare and life-threatening congenital heart condition, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, and would require multiple surgeries to survive.

The intended parents, who live in Los Angeles, opted to terminate the pregnancy.

But Ms. West, who lives in Alaska, refused to have an abortion. Instead, she went to Texas, which bans abortion, to seek specialists who could treat the baby’s defect.

On Wednesday, amid overlapping legal actions in the three states, Ms. West gave birth to a boy in Dallas whom activists have called “Baby Gabriel.” His legal parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, chose a different name.

“As if the heartbreak of his condition were not enough, they are devastated to see their family tragedy transformed into political theater by the Texas Attorney General’s office and McKenna West,” said a lawyer for the parents, Lee Budner, in a statement.

Mr. Budner said the boy was “now receiving medical care provided by a team of pediatric experts,” adding that the parents “would place their baby’s health and well-being first, following the advice of the baby’s medical team.”

Ms. West is seeking custody of the child.

The birth came just days after Mr. Paxton’s legal intervention on Monday. Mr. Paxton, a Republican locked in a tough race for the U.S. Senate, argued in Dallas County court that the parents were required to provide lifesaving care under Texas law.

“My office will use every tool available to protect innocent lives,” Mr. Paxton said in a statement.

The move sharply increased attention on what had already been a cause célèbre in anti-abortion circles this summer.

By Tuesday, Mr. Paxton celebrated having secured a temporary restraining order, or T.R.O., in Dallas that prevents the parents from removing the child from Texas until a hearing in late August. The order also requires them to provide “medically indicated, lifesaving treatment” to the baby.

At the same time, the Dallas County court also issued another restraining order against Ms. West. The order bars Ms. West from presenting herself as the baby’s parent, guardian or medical-decision maker “to anyone.”

“Unfortunately, because of the Texas T.R.O. that was entered yesterday, McKenna didn’t get to see or hold him after he was born,” Lincoln Wilson, a lawyer for Ms. West, said in an interview.

Ms. West, who did not respond to an interview request for this story, said in an interview this month with the former Fox News and current YouTube host Megyn Kelly that she did not support abortion and felt “trapped” by the surrogacy contract, which permitted the intended parents to end the pregnancy via abortion.

“It brought up a lot of fear,” said Ms. West, a nurse with two children of her own, in the interview.

Through a mutual friend, Ms. West connected with Lila Rose, the president of Live Action, an anti-abortion group. Ms. Rose said she helped Ms. West get legal support from the Alliance Defending Freedom, a prominent Christian conservative legal organization.

“There came a point where she, for the sake of her own medical care and safety, needed to travel to Texas, and so we did assist,” Ms. Rose said. “They were treating her baby like a product. The product had a defect, and so they were trying to send it back.”

Ms. Rose said that her organization does not support surrogacy, which “commoditizes human life” and leads to “heartbreaking and devastating situations like this.”

Mr. Wilson, the lawyer for Ms. West, said that the legal case was not over and that Ms. West would continue to fight for custody of the boy, who must undergo weeks of surgeries “before he’s really in the clear.”

item.title: The Debate Over Democrats’ Future Rages On After Hong’s Defeat in Wisconsin
item.description:
Francesca Hong was supposed to prove that a democratic socialist could win a statewide election.

Instead, her surprise loss in the primary election for governor of Wisconsin dealt a blow to the progressive movement and initiated a scramble among Democratic factions to define her narrow defeat either as an impressive harbinger of the movement’s future or an ominous sign of voter antipathy toward the far left.

Some prominent Democrats argued that the outcome was proof that the moderate wing of the party carried more electoral weight than the progressive one, which has dominated headlines this year as insurgent candidates have ousted incumbents in deep-blue cities.

Others, on the left, looked to celebrate the tight race — even though their candidate fell short — as evidence that progressives can compete in statewide contests.

“It’s a significant loss,” Robert Lasica, a spokesman for Madison’s Democratic Socialists of America chapter, said in an interview. But he argued the race was also “a big triumph of how far we can go with building the left infrastructure in Wisconsin that simply did not exist a year ago.”

David Crowley, who is the Milwaukee County executive and had briefly suspended his campaign just over a month ago, defeated Ms. Hong by a razor-thin margin. His victory defied months of polls that showed Ms. Hong far in the lead.

It was the second consecutive week with a Democratic primary in which a progressive candidate underperformed expectations. Last week in the Democratic Senate race in Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens, but the contest was closer than expected and was not called until the next morning. Both narrow outcomes have kept the debate that has been raging all year between moderates and progressives vigorously alive.

Mr. El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, and the D.S.A. is not officially part of the Democratic Party. But both the D.S.A. and non-D.S.A. progressives have roiled the party in this year’s midterms by exciting the left flank of the party’s base.

Some in the party hoped to export aspects of Ms. Hong’s success to other campaigns, notably her ground game. The former chef and restaurateur spent more time than any other candidate campaigning in rural Wisconsin, and it appeared to pay off with strong margins in some of those counties. Progressives have won a string of races partly on the strength of their ground games. The question is whether the model can be replicated without the populist policy proposals, such as abolishing I.C.E., that are resonating with some voters but that many moderates eschew.

The fallout of Ms. Hong’s campaign carries extra weight as the party eyes 2028, with those in each wing already jockeying to elevate their own. On Wednesday, Democrats openly exploring presidential bids sought to wield the election results to make their cases.

Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and former chief of staff to President Barack Obama, wrote on social media that Ms. Hong’s defeat showed “that the pragmatic wing isn’t a faction of this party. It’s the majority, it’s awake now, and it’s exerting itself.”

Representative Ro Khanna, a progressive congressman from California who had endorsed Ms. Hong and is also contemplating a run for president, sought to tamp down criticism of the far left.

“I appreciate that Democrats can have differences over single payer healthcare, free childcare, pausing data centers and other issues @FrancescaHongWI fought for,” he wrote on X. “But caricaturing and labeling candidates based on a few statements is not a politics I believe in.”

Democratic socialists had seen Wisconsin as a key opportunity to prove that their message could resonate in less liberal parts of the country. While they planned to study Ms. Hong’s loss to improve their electoral fortunes, several said they viewed Tuesday’s result as strong proof of the movement’s rise.

“Francesa won hundreds of thousands of votes — one of the highest vote totals of a democratic socialist candidate in any election in the United States,” said Katie Sims, a D.S.A. member in Ithaca, N.Y., who leads the group’s national electoral strategy. “Ultimately, it’s disappointing that she lost by such a small margin, but really heartening that it shows that these kinds of races are viable.”

D.S.A. members pointed to several areas for improvement. For one, the socialist infrastructure and campaign experience in Wisconsin was far less robust than in places such as New York City, which last fall elected Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, to be mayor. There, socialists had been building for years toward that victory as well as additional successes in congressional campaigns in June.

“For some people on the campaign, they have not worked at this scale yet before under these pressures,” Mr. Lasica said. “Next time around, we’re going to be in a better position.”

Some progressives criticized some of the biggest national names in their movement, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, for sitting out the race.

Ms. Hong also struggled in the final days of her campaign to explain past online remarks that were unearthed in news reports — including one in which she suggested canceling Thanksgiving.

Those reports unfurled an examination on the left, too, of how positions and rhetoric of pandemic-era progressivism have not always aged well with the broader population. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez jumped into that debate on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday, describing that era as “crazy” and “Woke 1.0” — a term that has become a political meme.

Asked about those comments on Wednesday and whether “Woke 1.0” was indeed crazy, Mr. Mamdani stressed that elected officials have a responsibility to own their evolving beliefs.

“I think that each person has a responsibility to tell New Yorkers, to tell Americans, when they’re running for office what they believe,” he said to reporters. “And sometimes what you believe can change, it can develop, it can grow.”

Dana Rubinstein and Tim Balk contributed reporting.

item.title: Federal Hate Crime Charge Filed in Stabbing of Muslim Man in Utah
item.description:
A man in Utah was indicted on a federal hate crime charge after he rode a scooter to a mall, bought a knife and repeatedly stabbed a Muslim man selling wares at a kiosk, the authorities said on Wednesday.

Federal prosecutors in Salt Lake City said Peter Larsen, 48, was indicted in connection with a stabbing on July 13 at the mall, in West Valley City. The victim was stabbed about a dozen times, on his head, chest and arms, causing internal bleeding, the authorities said, and a man who tried to intervene was also stabbed.

Mr. Larsen also faced state charges, including two counts of attempted aggravated murder and one count of having a dangerous weapon, according to the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office. It was not immediately clear what would happen with the state charges as the federal case proceeded.

“An alleged unprovoked attack on anyone in our community is unacceptable, but an attack allegedly motivated because of the victim’s religion is alarming,” the Salt Lake County district attorney, Sim Gill, said in a statement announcing the state charges.

Mr. Gill did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It was not clear whether Mr. Larsen had a lawyer. Mr. Larsen faces life in prison on the federal count, according to U.S. prosecutors.

The attack began when Mr. Larsen approached the victim and asked for water, according to a charging document filed by the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office. The authorities have said the ordeal was captured on the mall’s surveillance video and on witnesses’ cellphones.

Mr. Larsen asked the victim if he was Muslim, and after hearing that he was, Mr. Larsen said, “Everything is like Jesus Christ,” prosecutors said. He then began stabbing the man with a knife he had bought earlier that day, they said.

Several witnesses rushed toward Mr. Larsen and tried to subdue him. One person punched Mr. Larsen repeatedly, knocking him out, prosecutors said.

Another witness said he heard the victim calling for God and his mother.

Mr. Larsen told the authorities that he had planned to arrive at the mall and make an “exhibition of Muslims and hopefully be a catalyst so people would rid the country of Muslims,” prosecutors said.

Mr. Larsen also may have communicated with other people who shared his anti-Muslim beliefs, his brother told the authorities, according to prosecutors.

Witnesses told the authorities that Mr. Larsen approached other brown-skinned people in the mall and questioned their ethnicity and religious beliefs. The individuals who identified as Muslim worked behind a counter, rendering them inaccessible to Mr. Larsen, prosecutors said.

“Unfortunately for victim, he was working at a kiosk completely exposed and accessible,” they said.

Mr. Larsen will appear in court on Thursday in Salt Lake City. He has previous convictions of assaulting a police officer, arson and driving under the influence, prosecutors said.
